items.title: A pH electrode measures voltage, not chemistry
items.claim: A glass pH electrode gives a reading in pH units, but it doesn't 'detect acid'. It measures the voltage that develops across a thin glass membrane between the test solution and an internal reference — a voltage that is proportional to pH.
items.prompt: How does a glass membrane respond to pH?

options.text: The glass surface exchanges Na+ for H+ at its outer layer; the resulting potential difference between the two surfaces is set by the Nernst equation, giving 59 mV per pH unit at 25°C
It glows when acid is present
It vibrates at a frequency set by [H+]

items.reveal_title: Nernst equation makes the electrode work
items.reveal:
A pH electrode is a thin glass bulb filled with a known pH solution and a Ag/AgCl wire. The outside of the glass is in contact with the test solution. The two surfaces exchange ions differently depending on the H+ activity.

Nernst gives the potential: E = E0 + (RT/F) ln([H+]_test / [H+]_inside). At 25°C this is 0.0592 V per decade of [H+] — that is, 59 mV per pH unit.

Glass pH electrodes need calibration with buffer standards (typically pH 4 and pH 7) to set E0. They drift, age, and break easily — but they are the universal pH measurement standard, and the cheap colour-change of indicators is far less precise.
items.why: pH probes look like magic detectors. They are precision voltmeters reading voltages set by ion exchange at a glass surface.

items.title: A proton in an aromatic ring 'feels' a different magnetic field
items.claim: Switch on a strong magnetic field around a benzene ring and the circulating pi electrons generate their own magnetic field. Protons ATTACHED to the ring sit in a region where this ring current adds to the external field. Protons ABOVE the ring sit in a region where it subtracts.
items.prompt: What does this predict about NMR chemical shifts?

options.text: All aromatic protons appear at the same shift

Aromatic ring protons resonate at unusually high chemical shifts (~7 ppm); a proton positioned ABOVE the ring (as in 18-annulene's inner H's) appears at NEGATIVE shift — a diagnostic test for aromaticity
Aromatic protons don't appear in NMR spectra
Chemical shifts have nothing to do with the molecule's geometry

items.reveal_title: The ring current — aromaticity made visible
items.reveal:
In an aromatic ring, delocalised pi electrons circulate around the ring when placed in an external magnetic field. By Lenz's law this induces an opposing magnetic field that loops through the centre of the ring and outwards above and below.

Protons in the ring's plane (attached to the ring) sit where the induced field reinforces the external field — they are 'deshielded' and resonate at high chemical shift (~6 to 8 ppm).

In larger aromatic molecules like 18-annulene, the inner protons sit above the ring plane and experience the opposing component — their NMR signals appear at NEGATIVE chemical shift (around minus 3 ppm). This is the most direct physical evidence aromaticity exists.
items.why: Chemical shift is taught as a lookup table. It's really a probe of the molecule's three-dimensional electronic structure.

items.title: The 'heaviest stable element' was wrong for over a century
items.claim: Textbooks long stated that bismuth (element 83) was the heaviest stable element. In 2003 a French team measured bismuth-209 actually decaying — with a half-life of about 1.9 times 10 to the 19 years, around a billion times the age of the universe.
items.prompt: What now counts as the heaviest stable element?

options.text: Bismuth — the half-life is so long it doesn't matter
Lead-208 (element 82) is the heaviest nuclide with no detectable radioactivity; bismuth-209 is now classified as 'primordial but radioactive'
All elements above iron are unstable, eventually

items.reveal:
In 2003 de Marcillac and colleagues at the Institut d'Astrophysique Spatiale used scintillating bismuth germanate crystals as both source and detector to spot alpha decays of bismuth-209 to thallium-205.

The half-life is so long that a kilogram of bismuth produces only about 0.003 decays per second — easily missed by previous counting methods. Lead-208 ('doubly magic' with 82 protons and 126 neutrons) is now the heaviest truly stable nuclide.

Far more nuclei labelled 'stable' may simply have half-lives too long to have been measured yet. Stability is a statistical claim, not a chemical absolute.
items.why: Categories like 'stable' depend on how hard we have looked. Improved measurement reshuffles the periodic table's accepted facts.
